plan: Informative essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000047) on the Fresnel lighthouse lens: mirrors and soot, Fresnel's prism rings, lighter lens, Cordouan 1823, range and worldwide adoption. Topic checked against every bank (no matches). Ten new items, three aimed at hard (modifier placement, phrase-deletion effect, essay purpose). Plus E046-04 and E046-09 resubmitted as revision 2 on banked passage CLD-P-ACT-E-000046 (validator fixes only: trailing periods removed; placement item marked essay_level). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: Bending the Light
passages.text:
[1] Before the 1820s, most lighthouses used curved metal mirrors to aim the light of their lamps out to sea. [2] Even the best mirrors wasted much of that light, and keepers spent hours each day polishing away the soot that dimmed them.

[3] The French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel, {{9|who had spent years studying how light bends,}} proposed a different {{1|approach: a lens}} that would bend the light rather than reflect it. [4] A single solid lens big enough for a lighthouse would have been {{2|extremely heavy in weight}} and difficult to cast. [5] Fresnel's solution was to divide the lens into many small glass prisms. [6] {{4|Arranged in rings around a central lens, each prism}} bent a portion of the light into one strong horizontal beam. [7] The finished lens was far lighter {{3|then}} a solid lens of the same width.

[8] In 1823 the first Fresnel lens was installed in the Cordouan lighthouse in France. {{5|}} [9] The improvement was dramatic. [10] {{6|However,}} a light that had once been visible for only a few miles could now be seen from more than twenty miles away. [11] Within a few decades, Fresnel lenses {{7|has been installed}} in lighthouses around the world, and each lighthouse's lens was chosen to suit {{8|it's}} location.

passages.title: Painting by Number
passages.text:
[1] In the early 1950s, Dan Robbins, a commercial artist at the Palmer Paint Company in Detroit, was looking for a way to sell more of the company's paint. [2] He remembered reading that Leonardo da Vinci had sometimes numbered sections of a sketch so that his apprentices would know which colors to apply. [3] Robbins applied the same idea to {{1|a kit, it contained}} a board printed with a numbered outline and small pots of matching paint.

[4] The company's owner, Max Klein, was doubtful at first. [5] Early kits sold poorly, {{2|because}} store owners did not know where to display them. [6] Sales {{3|improved dramatically}} after a department store demonstration showed shoppers that anyone could finish a picture in a few evenings. [7] Within a few years, Palmer was selling millions of kits a year {{4|under the name Craft Master}}.

[8] Not everyone approved. [9] Critics complained that the kits turned painting into a mechanical {{5|task; following}} instructions rather than expressing ideas. [10] {{6|To them, a picture that came with its own instructions could not really be called art.}} [11] Robbins, however, argued that the kits, along with the simple instructions included in each box, {{7|was}} a first step toward painting for many people who had never held a brush.

[12] Today, paint-by-number pictures {{8|were}} sought by collectors, including some who once dismissed them. [13] In 2001 the Smithsonian Institution held an exhibition of the paintings, presenting them as a record of how ordinary Americans {{10|spent its}} leisure time in the years after World War II.

candidates.subskill: Colon before an explanatory noun phrase
candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: that would bend the light rather than reflect it
candidates.explanation: The colon follows a complete clause and introduces a phrase that explains what the different approach was.

B.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, but "a lens that would bend the light" is a phrase.

C.rationale: This leaves "A lens that would bend the light rather than reflect it" as a sentence fragment.

D.rationale: A comma alone joins two independent clauses, creating a comma splice.

hints: Is the part after the underline a complete sentence?

strategy.explanation: Check what can follow a semicolon or a period.

candidates.remember: A colon after a complete clause can introduce a phrase that explains it.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "Extremely heavy" says it once; the other choices repeat the idea of weight.

A.rationale: "Heavy" already refers to weight, so "in weight" is redundant.

D.rationale: This is wordy and repeats the idea of weight.

hints: Do any choices repeat an idea?

strategy.explanation: Pick the shortest version that keeps the meaning.

candidates.remember: Cut words that repeat what another word already says.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: "Lighter" makes a comparison, which is completed with "than."

A.rationale: "Then" refers to time; a comparison needs "than."

B.rationale: This keeps the time word "then" and adds "that of," which has nothing to refer to.

C.rationale: "Lighter as" is not a standard comparison.

hints: Is the sentence about time or a comparison?

strategy.explanation: Look for a comparative word such as "lighter."

candidates.remember: Use "than" for comparisons and "then" for time.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: Arranged in rings around a central lens, Fresnel made sure each prism
choices.C: Arranged in rings around a central lens, there was a prism that
choices.D: Arranged in rings around a central lens, the job of each prism was that it

candidates.evidence: bent a portion of the light into one strong horizontal beam
candidates.explanation: The prisms are what were arranged in rings, so "each prism" must come right after the introductory phrase.

B.rationale: Fresnel himself was not arranged in rings around a central lens.

C.rationale: The modifier has nothing it can logically describe; "there" was not arranged in rings.

D.rationale: A job cannot be arranged in rings; the modifier must describe the prisms.

hints: What was arranged in rings around a central lens?

strategy.explanation: Put the thing the modifier describes right after the comma.

candidates.remember: An introductory modifier describes the noun right after it.

candidates.stem:
At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence:
Cordouan stands on a small rocky island near the mouth of a river in southwestern France.
Should the writer make this addition here?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains why the Cordouan lighthouse was chosen to receive the first Fresnel lens.
choices.B: No, because it describes the lighthouse's setting, which is unrelated to the essay's focus on the lens.
choices.C: Yes, because it helps the reader understand how far the new light could be seen from the sea.
choices.D: No, because it contradicts the earlier statement that the first lens was installed in France.

candidates.evidence: In 1823 the first Fresnel lens was installed
candidates.explanation: The essay is about the lens and what it did. The island's location is unrelated, so the sentence would distract from the paragraph's point.

A.rationale: The sentence gives a location but no reason the lighthouse was chosen.

C.rationale: The sentence says nothing about how far the light could be seen.

D.rationale: The sentence agrees that Cordouan is in France.

strategy.explanation: State the focus, then test the sentence against it.

candidates.remember: Add a sentence only if it supports the paragraph's focus.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: could now be seen from more than twenty miles away
candidates.explanation: Sentence 9 makes a general claim (the improvement was dramatic), and sentence 10 gives a concrete example, so "For instance" fits.

A.rationale: Sentence 10 illustrates the improvement; it does not contrast with it.

B.rationale: "Nevertheless" signals a surprise despite the previous point, but the greater range is what the improvement would lead you to expect.

D.rationale: Nothing in sentence 10 replaces the improvement described in sentence 9.

hints: Does sentence 10 contrast with sentence 9 or illustrate it?

strategy.explanation: Label the relationship before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: Use "for instance" when a sentence gives an example of a general claim.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Within a few decades, Fresnel lenses
candidates.explanation: The plural subject "lenses" needs a plural verb, and "Within a few decades" places the action before a past point, so "had been installed" fits.

A.rationale: "Has" is singular, but the subject "lenses" is plural, and the present perfect does not fit a past account.

C.rationale: "Was" is singular and does not agree with "lenses."

D.rationale: "Is" is singular and present tense; the subject is plural and the account is in the past.

hints: What is the subject, and is it singular or plural?
candidates.remember: Match the verb to the subject's number and to the time of the passage.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The location belongs to each lighthouse, so the singular possessive "its" is correct.

A.rationale: "It's" means "it is," which makes no sense here.

C.rationale: "Their" is plural, but it refers to the singular "each lighthouse."

hints: Can you replace the word with "it is"?

candidates.stem: If the writer were to delete the underlined portion (adjusting the punctuation as needed), the essay would primarily lose:

choices.A: an explanation of how Fresnel's lens was manufactured in France.
choices.B: a description of the problems caused by soot on lighthouse mirrors.
choices.C: a detail suggesting why Fresnel could propose a new way to direct light.
choices.D: a comparison between Fresnel's ideas and those of other physicists.

candidates.explanation: The phrase tells the reader that Fresnel had studied how light bends, which explains why he could propose a lens that bends light.

A.rationale: The phrase concerns Fresnel's research, not manufacturing.

B.rationale: Soot is described in sentence 2, not in this phrase.

hints: How does the phrase connect to what Fresnel proposed?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the phrase adds to the sentence.

candidates.remember: A deleted phrase's value is the link it makes to the rest of the sentence.

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to describe how a scientific idea solved a practical problem. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it lists the many lighthouses around the world that first used Fresnel's lens design.
choices.B: Yes, because it shows how Fresnel's study of bending light produced a lighter, brighter lighthouse lens.
choices.C: No, because it focuses mainly on the daily work of keepers who polished the old lighthouse mirrors.
choices.D: No, because it never explains how Fresnel's lens directed light out to sea from the lighthouse.

candidates.evidence: bent a portion of the light into one strong horizontal beam
candidates.explanation: The essay identifies a practical problem (wasteful, heavy equipment), describes Fresnel's idea about bending light, and shows its result, which matches the purpose.

A.rationale: The essay names only one lighthouse and does not list others.

C.rationale: The keepers appear only in sentence 2; the essay focuses on the lens.

D.rationale: Sentence 6 explains that the prisms bent the light into a single horizontal beam.

hints: What problem does the essay start with, and how is it solved?

strategy.explanation: Trace the problem and the solution, then check each reason against the text.

candidates.remember: For purpose questions, the reason must be accurate and match the goal.

candidates.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined portion (ending the sentence with a period after the word year). Should the underlined portion be kept or deleted?

choices.A: Kept, because it explains why the kits began selling so much better than before
choices.B: Kept, because it identifies the brand name under which the kits were sold
choices.C: Deleted, because it repeats information that was already given earlier in the essay
choices.D: Deleted, because it contradicts the earlier statement that the early kits sold poorly

candidates.evidence: Within a few years, Palmer was selling millions of kits a year
candidates.explanation: The phrase adds a fact found nowhere else, the kits' brand name, so it should be kept.

A.rationale: The phrase names the brand; the reason for better sales is the demonstration in sentence 6.

C.rationale: The name Craft Master appears nowhere else in the essay.

D.rationale: Naming the brand does not contradict anything about early sales.

hints: What does the phrase add that the essay does not say elsewhere?

strategy.explanation: Decide what the phrase contributes, then check the reasons.

candidates.remember: A phrase worth keeping adds information the reader would otherwise lack.

candidates.stem: For the sake of logic and cohesion, sentence 5 should be placed:
candidates.explanation: The paragraph moves in time order: the owner's doubts, early poor sales, improved sales after a demonstration, and finally millions sold. Sentence 5 belongs where it is.

B.rationale: Sentence 6 explains how sales improved, so the poor early sales must come before it.

C.rationale: Placing the early poor sales after the report of millions sold breaks the time order.

D.rationale: Sentence 4 introduces the owner's doubts, which the poor early sales then bear out; reversing them loses that link.

hints: What order do the events in paragraph 2 happen in?

strategy.explanation: Put the events in time order.

candidates.remember: Sentence order should follow time or logic; check what each sentence depends on.
